title: Texas: the franchise exemption still needs a pre-offer notice

sections.heading: The exemption and the notice are separate

sections.heading: What the company secretary should prepare
paragraphs: Form 2703 asks for the franchisor’s legal name, all names under which it does or intends to do business, and principal business address. The FAQ lists a $25 fee. Its one-time notice has no expiry, but principal-address changes should be notified in writing.

Renaming the contract does not establish the exemption.

sections.heading: Do not confuse two filing tracks
paragraphs: The FAQ also describes registration, disclosures and update obligations for non-exempt business-opportunity sellers. Those are different from the one-time franchise exemption notice. If the company cannot establish the exemption conditions, leave the track unresolved instead of budgeting only $25.

paragraphs: Michigan section 445.1508 specifies ten business days before the earlier binding agreement or consideration, with the disclosure statement, prescribed notice and proposed agreements. The federal Rule has its separate 14-calendar-day disclosure requirement. One calculation must not silently replace the other.

sections.heading: Fictional scheduling problem
paragraphs: A Singapore service brand delivers documents shortly before a holiday period and plans a partner deposit two weeks later. The scheduler records the actual delivery method and receipt facts, the federal calendar calculation and a separate Michigan business-day calculation. The planned payment and signature each remain blocked until the relevant prerequisites are established.

sections.heading: A timing worksheet

rows: Michigan day-count method and holidays reviewed

sections.heading: Record uncertainty
paragraphs: This worksheet does not determine a legal delivery date or calculate holiday rules automatically. Unresolved receipt, amendment or negotiation facts should remain named questions, not a green permission indicator.

practicalOutput: A dual-clock disclosure worksheet.

title: Can Minnesota initial franchise fees fund pre-opening support?
description: Use the actual financial-assurance condition to model when money becomes available.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The answer depends on the condition
paragraphs: Minnesota’s published guidance describes escrow, impoundment, surety-bond and fee-deferral arrangements where the financial review requires assurance. If the applicable arrangement delays receipt or release until opening or another condition, the same fee cannot fund earlier cash costs unless separate available capital bridges the timing.

sections.heading: Fictional cash illustration
paragraphs: Assume, solely for planning, that a brand must pay $12,000 for training travel and wages in month one while an initial fee becomes available in month three. The pre-opening funding task is the dated $12,000 outflow and any other actual outflows, reduced only by committed receipts available in those months. Do not count both an expense and an identical arbitrary reserve as two different costs.

sections.heading: What the CFO should document
bullets: Exact financial condition and its release trigger.
Support obligations with payment dates.
Cash actually available before release.
Alternative funding evidence, cost and constraints.
Release evidence and responsible person.
Downside opening-date assumption.

sections.heading: Scope
paragraphs: The illustrative amount is invented and is not a Minnesota fee or required reserve. This guide does not predict an examiner’s condition. Use the actual order/agreement and reviewed guidance in the cash model.

practicalOutput: A dated support-funding bridge.
